name: AI Instructions Relay Cartridge
summary: Reusable, AI/platform-agnostic instruction memory for AI-assisted development using RelayDB project-memory artifacts.
reachability_policy: The root instruction cartridge intentionally links to every otherwise-unreachable node so an AI traversal starting at this anchor can discover the full instruction graph.

summary: Project context should be authored, reviewed, compiled, verified, versioned, navigable, and shared as a repository-native artifact.
AI coding tools often start without the full project story, causing repeated explanation, rediscovery, stale assumptions, and unsafe edits.
The AI should understand what it is touching before it changes it.
Do not let AI write code and disappear. Make it leave behind structured project memory for the next developer, branch, release, and AI session.
Stable anchors give important project facts durable identities that humans and AI can reference directly.
Explicit relationships connect functions, modules, risks, decisions, tests, branches, and concepts so an AI can see what is connected and why.
Provenance records where a fact, decision, or behavior came from, such as a module, branch, issue, release, or upstream concept.
RelayDB memory should compile into artifacts that can be checked for physical integrity, anchor consistency, and graph health.
Branch memory records durable engineering facts from a branch: changed files/functions, decisions, risks, tests, side effects, and migration notes.
A versioned .relay artifact can act as a release-specific memory cartridge for a project, preserving context for that exact version.
RelayDB memory should be useful to humans and AI through the same source of structured project facts rather than separate memory systems.
Tagged JSONL source memory is the editable truth source. Compiled .relay memory is the verified navigable artifact. If source memory is newer, compiled memory may be stale.

name: Anchor
summary: Stable identity for a memory node. Every important project fact should have a durable # anchor.

name: Provenance
summary: Origin, source, parent, module, branch, release, or upstream context for a memory node.

name: Relationship
summary: Related nodes, affected areas, side effects, dependencies, tests, risks, or concepts connected to a memory node.

name: Aliases
summary: Search terms, alternate names, retrieval hints, and human-friendly phrases that should locate the node later.
Human + AI work on project, AI drafts tagged JSONL memory, RelayDB compiles it, artifact is verified, and future AI sessions read memory first.
Before making code changes, the AI must read project instructions, source memory, compiled memory if available, README, branch goal, and relevant source files.
Before editing, the AI must summarize project purpose, relevant architecture, known risks, related modules/functions, likely side effects, tests, and memory nodes that may need updates.

During work, the AI tracks durable engineering facts only: files changed, functions changed, APIs changed, binary format changes, CLI changes, decisions, risks, tests, side effects, and documentation updates needed.
Before commit, generate branch memory JSONL that records durable engineering facts from the branch using the RelayDB 4-tag format.
Compile source memory into a .relay artifact, verify physical integrity, audit graph health, jump into important anchors, patch memory holes, recompile, and verify again.
Before implementing a feature, compile current memory, inspect project context, identify affected areas, risks, tests, memory updates, and decide branch scope.
Before interacting with a RelayDB-enabled project, read AI instruction memory and human-readable instruction files before interpreting project memory.
Inspect tagged JSONL source memory and compiled .relay memory if available before planning or editing.
Do not edit code until the AI has loaded relevant project memory and produced an impact summary.
Before code changes, produce an impact summary covering affected files/functions, risks, side effects, tests, and memory updates.
Do not record raw chat, private conversation, irrelevant commentary, secrets, credentials, personal data, or casual discussion in RelayDB memory.
RelayDB memory should capture durable engineering facts, not conversational noise.
AI may draft memory, but human or maintainer review is required before treating memory as approved release/project memory.
If source memory or source files changed after the .relay artifact was compiled, warn that compiled memory may be stale and recommend recompilation.
Identify and preserve project invariants before changing code. Invariants may include binary format layout, public APIs, compiler/reader contracts, security boundaries, and test assumptions.
AI may introduce bugs by editing code without understanding hidden dependencies, side effects, prior decisions, related tests, or architectural constraints.
If AI-generated memory is not reviewed, RelayDB could compile inaccurate or hallucinated project facts into a trusted-looking artifact.

Critical memory or artifact issues should block trust or merge until fixed. Examples include invalid JSONL, duplicate anchors, broken internal references, failed physical integrity, and unsafe stale-memory conditions.
Warning-level issues should be reviewed but may not block work. Examples include orphan nodes, external references, stale aliases, undocumented tests, or missing helpful relationships.
Informational audit findings provide useful context such as high-frequency hubs, graph statistics, or suggested improvements.
Compile tagged JSON/JSONL source memory into a .relay artifact.
Verify physical integrity of a compiled .relay artifact before trusting it.
Audit source memory for duplicates, missing references, orphans, external refs, cycles, and other graph-health issues.
Navigate a compiled .relay artifact starting from a stable anchor.
Generate an AI startup packet from instruction and project memory cartridges, including rules, integrity status, architecture, invariants, risks, and safe next steps.
AI role cartridges define reusable AI behaviors, safeguards, skills, output styles, and task constraints that can be combined with project-memory cartridges.
Security-focused AI mode that reviews authentication, input validation, secrets, dependency risks, unsafe data exposure, and secure defaults before proposing changes.
forbidden_actions: rewrite unrelated code unless explicitly asked
required_output_format: Rank findings by severity and include evidence, affected anchors, and suggested mitigations.

summary: Rust-focused refactor assistant that checks ownership, borrowing, lifetimes, error handling, module boundaries, public APIs, and compiler/reader contracts before edits.
Teaching-focused AI mode that explains concepts in plain English, uses examples and mental models, avoids unexplained jargon, and scaffolds learning step by step.
Documentation-focused AI mode that updates README files, guides, API docs, examples, diagrams, and branch memory while preserving technical accuracy.
Review-focused AI mode that examines correctness, tests, edge cases, spec drift, unsafe assumptions, and hidden dependencies without rewriting code unless asked.
forbidden_actions: approve behavior without tests or reasoning
required_output_format: List findings by severity with evidence, affected files, likely impact, and recommended next action.

summary: Branch node records branch goal, scope, changed areas, related decisions, risks, tests, and aliases.
Function node records stable function identity, file path, purpose, inputs/outputs, affected functions, related tests, risks, and aliases.
Decision node records accepted/rejected/pending decisions, rationale, provenance, affected code, risks, and migration notes.
Risk node records known risks, causes, affected anchors, severity, mitigations, and related tests.
Test node records what behavior a test protects, which functions/modules it covers, commands to run it, and known gaps.
Invariant node records project rules that must not be broken, such as binary layout, public API contracts, command behavior, or security boundaries.
Plan node records feature planning context before implementation: goals, affected areas, risks, tests, branch split, and memory updates required.
If a compiled .relay artifact is available, verify its physical integrity before treating it as authoritative project memory.
If project memory is missing, unreadable, contradictory, corrupted, or cannot be verified, stop and ask for clarification before editing code.
Never store secrets, credentials, tokens, private keys, raw passwords, session tokens, sensitive personal data, or proprietary confidential data in RelayDB memory.
Do not invent project facts. Memory entries must be grounded in source files, verified artifacts, human-approved decisions, or clearly labeled inferences.
When generating memory, clearly distinguish facts observed in source files or verified artifacts from inferences, assumptions, suggestions, or plans.
Ask for explicit approval before deleting files, removing public APIs, rewriting large sections, changing generated artifacts, or performing destructive project actions.
Do not change public APIs, CLI command behavior, exported functions, file formats, or external contracts without first producing an impact summary.
Do not change binary formats, source-memory schemas, jump-table layout, anchor semantics, or compiled artifact structure without a migration plan and compatibility notes.
Behavior-changing code edits should include or identify tests that protect the changed behavior, or explain why tests are not applicable.
If architecture, public APIs, protocol behavior, file layout, CLI commands, risks, or invariants change, update RelayDB source memory before treating the work as complete.
Prefer small, reviewable, reversible edits. Avoid broad rewrites unless explicitly requested and justified by the impact analysis.
If memory nodes, source files, README, or compiled artifacts contradict each other on important behavior, stop and surface the contradiction before editing.
If the AI environment does not have a native RelayDB reader, read RELAY_FILE_READER_INSTRUCTIONS.md before attempting to parse a .relay artifact.
Command node records setup, build, test, lint, format, run, verify, audit, and deployment commands for a project.
Evidence node records whether a memory fact is observed, inferred, human-approved, generated, planned, or deprecated, and where that evidence came from.
API contract node records exported functions, CLI commands, public behavior, expected inputs/outputs, compatibility promises, and breaking-change risks.
Migration node records how to move from one format, API, command, schema, or artifact version to another while preserving compatibility where possible.
Relay reader protocol node records how to safely parse a .relay file: pointer offset, header assumptions, jump table parsing, payload decoding, and integrity checks.

When an AI has only uploaded .relay files and no native RelayDB reader, it should read the Markdown reader instructions, use the provided minimal reader code, verify anchors, then inspect required startup anchors.
